newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican Telkom privatisation on track for April.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican Telkom privatisation on track for April.

text.p: South Africa expects binding bids for a 30 percent stake in its Telkom communications company in February, but finalisation of the first major privatisation deal could slip into April, an official said on Thursday.

Posts and Telecommunications Ministry spokesman Connie Molusi said the four finalists were preparing proposals in a phase that involved regular contact to check details of the South African tender offer.
"The programme is quite tight. It's not likely that a decision will be made before the budget on the 12th of March, but a decision will be announced not later than April.
"Implementation of the deal will start very soon after the announcement," Molusi said.

The partial privatisation of Telkom, which posted an operating profit of 1.8 billion rand on turnover of 7.9 billion rand in the half year to September 30, will be the first test of the government's announced intention to partially or fully privatise a number of state enterprises.
South Africa narrowed the race in December to four companies, inviting firm bids by Deutsche Telkom, France Telecom, Telekom Malaysia and South Western Bell (SBC) of the United States.
Telkom Malaysia and SBC announced shortly afterwards that they would bid as a consortium, a route that Minister of Posts and Telecommunications Jay Naidoo said he would prefer.
South Africa is offering a 20 to 30 percent equity stake in Telkom. Sources close to the negotiations say all the bids are likely to be for the full 30 percent stake.
A further 10 percent will be offered to black-led investors representing the majority disadvantaged under apartheid.
"We're expecting the three binding bids sometime in February. We will choose one or more preferred bidders for a final round of talks leading to an announcement by April," Molusi said.
Telkom managing director Brian Clark said in December that he expected a decision by the end of March.

Director general of communications Andile Ngcaba last year estimated the cash value of the deal at five to six billion rand with a total value, including technology transfers and training, of up to seven billion rand.
Ministry sources say now, however, that figure could be inaccurate and that the non-cash component could form a larger proportion of an agreement.
